task_reconstruction.decision: Advise George R. R. Martin whether three dragons can be sustained across climates and what ecological and human support consequences follow.

contributions.summary: Combines 45 region objects, individual dragon state, resources, migration, reproduction, and intervention in a daily ABM.
Compresses five regional factors into a suitability value that routes settlement and movement.
Makes hunting, gold, den, reproduction, health, mass, forest, and ice consequences explicit.
Couples single-dragon mass, deer, and vegetation through three nonlinear ODEs.
Contrasts population outcomes under thresholded dragon removal and forest restoration.
Uses trajectory sweeps to identify prey-growth, hunting, damage, and growth-rate regimes.
Translates metabolic demand into deer counts and an illustrative one-year stock area.

edges.handoff: Region climate class and habitat factors supply the daily suitability inputs.
Suitability and the region graph trigger and constrain migration.
The temperature draw contributes to migration through suitability.
Agent health, gold, and den state enter mining and settlement transitions.
Agent mass enters the allometric prey-demand rule.
Agent health, fullness, age, and mass enter daily reproduction and state updates.
Den acquisition and mining cost gate later reproduction and survival.
Hunting success changes fullness, health, and the subsequent weight bin.
Migration selects the next ecoregion whose resources define a new suitability score.
Dragon population and habitat damage activate the management scenario.
Age-dependent hunting efficiency enters food intake and mass growth.
Dragon mass and hunting efficiency determine prey predation.
Dragon mass determines vegetation damage.
Prey count feeds back into dragon food availability.
The mature dragon state supplies the prey and vegetation sign analysis.
The prey equation supplies the mature per-capita threshold.
The vegetation equation supplies the mature per-capita threshold.
The dragon derivative is discretized by forward Euler.
The prey derivative is discretized by forward Euler.
The vegetation derivative is discretized by forward Euler.
Allometric food demand supplies the zoo prey conversion.

assumptions.summary: Dragons are born at 10 kg, reach about 250 kg after one year, and continue growing through life.
Dragons may reproduce sexually or asexually after satisfying age, health, gold, and den conditions.
All prey animals are represented as deer for the regional model and resource conversion.
A dragon can move across one ecoregion in one day.
Dens, forest, gold, temperature, and prey can be normalized and combined into one suitability score.
The regional ecosystem is assumed stable before one dragon enters as the sole dominant predator.
Reptile allometry is assumed to represent fictional dragon metabolic demand.
Food availability multiplicatively modulates logistic growth toward 6000 kg.
Deer grow exponentially and dragon predation scales with normalized dragon mass.
Vegetation can be represented as one proportion with exponential growth and dragon damage.
A one-month forward Euler step is assumed adequate for the coupled system.
Human assistance can remove at most one dragon and restore forest when a threshold is crossed.
One deer-energy equivalent and one deer-density estimate transfer across dragon weights and management settings.
Captivity is treated as the practical response once wild ecological damage appears severe.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Biological analogues supply reptile metabolism, Komodo reproduction, lizard growth, deer calories, and zoo-resource proxies, but transfer quality differs by source.
The world is discretized into 45 region objects, each assumed traversable within one day.
Temperature, dens, gold, forest, and prey initialize each ecoregion; distributions and units are incompletely documented.
Each prey item receives an abstract calorie rating between zero and ten and increments daily until deletion above ten.
The regional model fixes c=0.856, r_opt=0.035, w_max=6000 kg, b=0.889, j=0.25, l=0.09, g=0.2, e_0=0.1, and e_max=0.5.
The regional run starts at w_0=10 kg, p_0=5000 deer, and v_0=0.5 with maturity at 21 years.
Captivity calculations report deer/year ranges across maximum masses, including 158 to 2627 at 250 kg.
Zoo resource equivalents compare prey quantities but do not provide a labor or community production ledger.
Twenty-one references mix fiction, biology, web resources, modeling precedents, and management applications.
Recipe images and playful population-control text are visually distinct from technical evidence and lack full source attribution.
The hunting law uses a=139065, b=0.889, 365 days/year, and 5000 calories per prey-equivalent.
The ODE uses k=119040 kcal/deer and c=k/a=0.856 kg^b/deer, unlike the ABM's random zero-to-ten prey ratings.

models.summary: normalized five-factor ecoregion suitability: Compress den availability, forest, temperature, gold, and prey into the daily ABM habitat score.
stochastic seasonal temperature generator: Generate a daily climate draw from season and climate-class inputs for suitability and movement decisions.
agent state and initialization ledger: Define the individual dragon state that the daily ABM transitions update.
gold acquisition and den settlement transitions: Represent resource-gated den establishment and its health cost.
allometric daily prey-demand rule: Convert dragon mass to a whole-prey daily hunting requirement.
threshold-triggered adjacent-cell migration: Move an unsettled or poorly matched dragon between connected ecoregions.
daily event and binned-state transition system: Update reproduction, health, and mass after daily agent activities.
thresholded removal and habitat restoration control: Represent the ABM management scenario that removes dragons and restores damaged forest.
food-modulated logistic dragon growth ODE: Couple a single dragon's mass growth to food availability, metabolic need, prey count, and an age-dependent hunting coefficient.
age-dependent piecewise hunting efficiency: Increase hunting effectiveness linearly from hatchling to maturity and hold it fixed thereafter.
dragon-coupled exponential prey ODE: Update the regional deer count under intrinsic exponential growth and dragon predation.
dragon-coupled vegetation proportion ODE: Update the regional vegetation state under exponential growth and dragon damage.
late-time sign thresholds and structural regime test: Expose why mature prey and vegetation decline thresholds coincide with chosen rate parameters.
forward Euler integration and one-at-a-time sweep: Advance the coupled dragon, prey, and vegetation system and compare selected parameter trajectories.
calorie-to-prey-to-stock-area conversion: Translate modeled dragon food need into deer counts, zoo resources, and a one-year stock-area estimate.

verification.summary: The five-factor suitability interface and full 45-row region ledger were checked against the rendered page.
The stochastic temperature, hunting-demand, gold, den, and truncated migration interfaces were checked at original resolution.
Reproduction, health, weight, forest, and ice costs were cross-read between prose and Table 2.
Equations (1)-(3) were checked from the page image; the final growth factor is c p/w^b.
Every listed regional parameter and initial condition was mapped back to its model interface.
All five threshold/count pairs in Table 3 were retained with their 100-day horizon.
The vegetation transition was recomputed from lambda_v=l-g and compared with the plotted sweep.
The prey transition was recomputed from lambda_p=j-e_max and compared with the plotted sweep.
The 58-square-mile result was reproduced as 2647/45=58.8 and classified as stock rather than sustainable area.
The 2647 letter value, 2666 body value, 158-2627 restricted range, and initial-versus-maximum-weight wording were compared.
The deer-calorie citation was identified as a human cannibalism calorific-content source rather than direct deer calorimetry.
The appendix's ice-loss extremes were retained as selected scenarios rather than probability bounds.
The post-den gold rule was compared with the alternative run and the authors' realism admission.
Changing b without refitting a_m was recorded as a unit-scale limitation.
The r_opt sweep was retained without upgrading one-at-a-time trajectories to joint uncertainty validation.
All 31 nonempty physical-page text segments and all rendered pages were included in the read and visual review ledger.
Evaluating S=0 and S=4 gives arctic/temperate/tropical winter lower bounds of -16/-12/-8 degrees C and summer maxima of 16/33/50 degrees C.
The a=139065, b=.889 ceiling law was independently evaluated at six masses from 10 to 6000 kg.
A starving ABM hatchling's forced 0.25 kg/day gain produces at least 101.25 kg after one year, conflicting with the 30-40 kg official anchor.
A one-month forward-Euler implementation reproduces the reported 50-year mass and prey endpoint closely.
At the reproduced endpoint, modeled hunting and metabolic need differ by roughly a factor of 1527, revealing the no-prey mass-freeze structure.
Monthly Euler gives maximum deer counts near 2648/2815/3226/4106/4993/7557, not the printed 2627/2793/3200/4074/4954/7507.
Direct a w^b/k values are about 158.23/293.03/542.66/1004.94/1441.07/2668.71 deer/year.
The letter's 2647/45 is 58.82 square miles, requiring upward rounding and explicit multiplication for three dragons.

results_trace.summary: The selected stochastic run spreads dragons unevenly across connected ecoregions and produces clustering around favorable resources.
Continued reproduction and resource transitions produce a high-population scenario with major forest and ice effects.
At day 100, thresholds 50, 100, 200, 400, and 1000 yield 2, 0, 39, 42, and 40 dragons in single runs.
The selected coupled trajectory makes dragon mass increase while prey and vegetation eventually decline.
The paper reports that prey growth near or above 15 percent can sustain a target fraction of maximum dragon mass.
Larger initial herds delay scarcity but do not repair the structural absence of prey carrying capacity.
The qualitative transition occurs near g=l=0.09, matching the mature sign threshold.
The qualitative prey transition occurs near e_max=j=0.25, matching the mature sign threshold.
The body table reports 2666 deer/year for its largest full-grown scenario, while the letter reports 2647.
At a 250 kg maximum, the paper reports 158 deer/year minimum and 2627 maximum.
Dividing 2647 deer by 45 deer per square mile yields about 58.8 square miles of one-year standing stock.
Zoo tables frame food provision as institutionally imaginable but do not calculate assistance community size.
The ABM outcome is highly sensitive to permanent den acquisition and continued gold mining behavior.
The authors acknowledge that region size and deer density are absent from the ODE.
Extreme settings produce a broad range of global ice-loss outcomes rather than a replicated probability distribution.
Stopping mining after den acquisition creates a much larger population, so the retained baseline rule constrains results artificially.
At dragon masses 10, 30, 40, 100, 250, and 6000 kg, the allometric ceiling gives 1, 2, 3, 5, 11, and 175 prey-equivalents per day.
Monthly Euler gives about 39.05 kg at year 1; at year 50 it gives w=5997.81 kg, p=3.495 deer, and v=0.00752.
At year 50 the reconstructed actual hunt is about 1.747 deer/year while metabolic need is about 2667.84 deer/year, yet mass remains near the cap.
The minimum deer rows follow a w^b/k conversion closely, while the maximum rows do not match the declared monthly Euler scheme.
Using 2647 deer and 45 deer/square mile gives 58.82 square miles for one consumed annual stock and about 176.47 square miles for three.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: J: A two-scale capsule is judge-friendly when every headline preserves entity, unit, horizon, and scenario.
J: Stakeholder translation is useful only when it preserves the same validated scenario ledger as the body.
C: A compact activity table makes an agent model inspectable, but prose/table conflicts must be resolved before implementation.
J: Threshold outcomes are memorable only with units, repeated runs, uncertainty, costs, and a decision rule.
C: A calorie-to-prey conversion is not yet a sustainable land or assistance-community model.

weaknesses.summary: The suitability expression is an equal average, although the prose calls it a weighted sum and publishes no weights.
The five normalized factors have no complete unit and normalization ledger, so the score cannot be independently reproduced.
Forty-five cells are said to be traversable in a day, but no area, distance, geometry, or adjacency matrix is reported.
Random region inputs are not accompanied by distributions, random seeds, repeated runs, or calibration observations.
The seasonal-temperature notation does not unambiguously identify the two uniform draws or their dependence.
No hemisphere mapping or season-transition process explains how S changes through the year.
The 50 degree cap is imposed without a lower cap, validation distribution, or temporal autocorrelation.
One passage says the initial dragons are no older than one year, while another initializes ages from one to four years.
The initial state omits sex, energy reserve, injury, lineage, and uncertainty despite later reproduction and health claims.
The model continues mining after a den has been found; Appendix A admits stopping is more realistic but would increase population.
Gold has no physical unit, depletion law, replenishment process, or independent validation.
Mining costs health, but the health scale, cap, mortality boundary, and energy interpretation are not defined.
A 50 percent independent daily den-find probability is assumed without evidence or den-capacity accounting.
The reptile allometric relation is extrapolated to dragon masses without uncertainty or a documented unit conversion.
Metabolism excludes flight, fire, hunting, migration, reproduction, trauma, thermoregulation, and recovery.
The ABM prey calorie rating runs from 0 to 10, but the hunting conversion assumes 5,000 calories per prey with no bridge.
Taking a ceiling forces at least one prey-equivalent per day for every positive mass, distorting low-demand agents.
The prose says hunting removes one forest unit per prey while Table 2 says ten, leaving environmental damage ambiguous.
The 0.1 suitability trigger is chosen without calibration, sensitivity, or stated false-migration cost.
The migration sentence is truncated at the page boundary, so the actual destination-choice rule is not recoverable.
Migration has no distance, time, flight-energy, route-risk, or climate-transition cost.
A 25 percent daily reproduction probability corresponds to roughly 91 event opportunities per year and is justified only by clutch size.
Sexual reproduction lacks partner pairing and double-counting rules; asexual reproduction lacks a calibrated biological rate.
Health increases by 15 daily without a stated upper bound, making long-lived agents accumulate an unphysical reserve.
Activity costs, forest costs, and prose descriptions are not reconciled into one executable ledger.
Fixed fullness-bin changes of 0.25 or 0.5 kg/day are not calibrated to the official one-year mass anchor.
The ABM weight transition is structurally incompatible with the regional food-modulated logistic ODE.
The intervention threshold has no unit or baseline maximum, so Table 3 cannot be replicated from the prose.
The 100-day outcomes are single stochastic runs: threshold 50 gives 2 dragons, 100 gives 0, 200 gives 39, 400 gives 42, and 1000 gives 40.
Restoration has no workforce, cost, production, land, or assistance-level state and therefore is not a community-size model.
Removing at most one dragon and restoring forest are asserted management capabilities without feasibility constraints.
Food availability enters both the realized growth coefficient and the separate supply-demand factor, creating double counting.
The multiplicative food ratio can reverse growth, but its units and mapping to prey dynamics are not derived.
The realized growth coefficient treats food intake as both a rate modifier and a later growth-sign modifier.
The regional metabolism coefficient and exponent are not accompanied by a fully reproducible source-unit conversion.
Food eaten is proportional to prey count and dragon mass without region area, prey density, handling time, or saturation.
The final visually checked factor is c p/w^b, not its reciprocal; the paper does not establish its dimensional closure.
At w=w_max the logistic factor is zero, so an adult at the cap cannot lose mass even when food collapses.
With w_0=10 kg and w_max=6000 kg, the ODE no longer enforces the official one-year 250 kg anchor.
The linear rise from e_0=0.1 to e_max=0.5 at age 21 is selected without hunting observations.
The efficiency law omits learning variation, senescence, injury, prey defense, habitat, and season.
The prey equation has exponential growth and no carrying capacity, contradicting the claimed stable pre-entry ecosystem.
When the dragon is mature, the prey sign is controlled by j-e_max=0.25-0.5<0, so decline is built into parameter choice.
Prey count is continuous and can become negative under explicit Euler without a nonnegativity event.
The predation term is not reconciled with the energy intake used in the dragon growth equation.
Vegetation is defined as a proportion but plotted near 2, 7, and 40, outside the physical interval [0,1].
The vegetation equation has exponential growth and no carrying capacity despite the stable-baseline assumption.
At mature mass, l-g=0.09-0.2<0, so vegetation extinction is largely predetermined by coefficient signs.
The vegetation state omits deer grazing, climate, area, biomass units, and restoration feedback.
The e_max transition occurs near j=0.25 because the prey per-capita sign changes there; this is a structural identity, not external validation.
The g transition occurs near l=0.09 because the vegetation per-capita sign changes there; calling it a bifurcation overstates the evidence.
No positive coexistence equilibrium, Jacobian, stability domain, or uncertainty interval is established.
Forward Euler uses a one-month step without a time-unit reconciliation against derivatives stated per year.
No step-halving or convergence test shows that the dragon trajectory is numerically stable.
No positivity projection or event prevents deer population from crossing below zero.
No bounded-state treatment prevents vegetation proportion from exceeding one or becoming negative.
One-at-a-time sweeps omit parameter interactions, joint uncertainty, stochastic replication, and decision-reversal frequency.
The letter labels 2,647 deer/year as the full-grown requirement, but that value corresponds to a 12-year mass; Table 4 reports 2,666 for the full-grown case.
For a 250 kg cap, Table 4 reports a minimum of 158 and maximum of 2,627 deer/year without reconciling those regimes to welfare or control.
The prose says different initial weights are compared, while the table header varies maximum weight.
Maximum feeding outputs are described as observed feeding in the wild even though they are model-generated.
The 58 square miles is a one-year stock division, and the paper concedes no deer remain for the next year; it is not sustainable area.
The letter's 58-square-mile figure is for one annual deer stock, not a three-dragon land requirement.
The zoo table compares food quantities but never computes community population, labor, productivity, infrastructure, or assistance scenarios.
Reference [6] is a human cannibalism calorific-content paper rather than direct deer calorimetry.
The conclusion recommends captivity without an explicit optimization over ecological risk, welfare, cost, and support capacity.
Recipe pages use several images without source attribution, raising the official unauthorized-image concern.
The letter's climate advice is mainly qualitative and lacks consistent arid, warm-temperate, and arctic numerical resource comparisons.
The required community size under different levels of assistance is never modeled.
Real-world applications are named, but mechanism match and calibration to whale sharks, deer management, or wildlife ABMs are not demonstrated.
Independent range evaluation gives tropical winter temperatures down to -8 degrees C and arctic/tropical summer ranges up to 16/50 degrees C; no climate data validate these distributions.
The symbol T is reused for both the temperature function and the suitability normalization maximum, obscuring the interface.
The paper alternately describes three full-grown, mature, no-older-than-one-year, and one-to-four-year initial dragons with masses of 30-100 kg.
The prey rating increments daily and is deleted above ten, but the method never supplies a reproducible prey reproduction transition.
Even a starving juvenile gains 0.25 kg/day, so a 10 kg hatchling reaches at least 101.25 kg in one year, contradicting the official 30-40 kg anchor.
The paper says strict biological guidelines are conserved, but the ABM fixed mass bins and regional logistic ODE use incompatible growth and prey-energy mechanisms.
Because Equation (1) also has an outer factor p, dw/dt approaches zero as prey approaches zero; starvation freezes mass instead of producing loss or death.
A monthly-Euler reconstruction gives w about 5998 kg and p about 3 at 50 years, yet actual hunting is only about 1.75 deer/year against roughly 2668 deer/year metabolic need.
The Table 4 maximum deer counts do not match the declared one-month Euler scheme and are closer to a hidden fine-step or continuous calculation.
At 6000 kg the formula gives about 2668.7 deer/year; the table's 2666 is closer to the not-yet-full 15-year mass around 5992.6 kg.
The 2647/45 calculation is 58.82 square miles and should round upward to at least 59; three one-year stocks require roughly 176-178 square miles before sustainability.
The conclusion calls the regional system one-predator/multiple-prey, but Equation (2) has only one aggregate deer state.
Climate recommendations shift among semi-arid, tropical, wetter temperate, and tropical-to-semi-arid preferences without a controlled migration comparison.
The conclusion presents sea-ice melting as general even though Appendix A ranges from complete Antarctic loss to mild or no loss in fully frozen cells.
Temperature affects ABM suitability but not metabolism, energy demand, health, or the regional ODE, so climate-energy claims are disconnected.
Figure 9's caption states a transition between .05 and .01; the ordered interval and body discussion indicate .05 to .10.
Figure 8's legend includes an extra 1000 series and an irregular order that is not reconciled with the stated initial-prey scenarios.

independent_extensions.summary: Replace 45 one-day cells with georeferenced areas, distances, adjacency, habitat capacity, and movement-energy costs.
Rebuild the ABM as an executable transition ledger with seeds, replicated runs, event logs, calibrated reproduction, bounded health, and conserved prey energy.
Replace doubled food modulation with a dimensionally closed intake-assimilation-maintenance-activity-growth balance.
Bound prey and vegetation with area-dependent carrying capacities, density-based encounter, climate productivity, and nonnegative states.
Use an adaptive nonnegative solver, step convergence, equilibrium analysis, and uncertainty propagation.
Map assistance levels to food production, labor productivity, households, infrastructure, risk, restoration, and community population.
Replace standing-stock division with a sustainable deer recruitment and habitat-productivity land model for one and three dragons.
Run global sensitivity and stochastic decision-reversal analysis over allometry, ecology, reproduction, intervention, climate, and numerical settings.
